demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
Watching TV programmes/ films or reading about similar events

Threat.value: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over

Negative Appraisals.value: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: For an index trauma of unexpected/traumatic death of a loved one, 'betrayal by someone I trusted' is a poor fit unless the death involved clear interpersonal wrongdoing by a trusted person; nothing else in the profile supports that specific circumstance, so this item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type.

issues.item: Threat: Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
issues.explanation: 'Need to stay alert' at bedtime implies ongoing external danger, which is less coherent with bereavement-related trauma in the absence of any triggers or appraisals about current interpersonal/physical threat. The rest of the profile centers on loss, self-blame, fragmented reliving memory, and catastrophic interpretations of delay, making this item stand out as mismatched.

vignette:
Adama was twenty-three years old, an environmental scientist who spent her days analyzing soil samples in a bright, quiet laboratory. She had moved from West Africa to the United States for graduate school two years earlier, and she had built a life around precision and order. That was what made what happened feel so impossible. Her younger brother, Kofi, had been visiting her for the first time. He was nineteen, and she had been so proud to show him her world. One evening, after a long day of fieldwork, she had asked him to pick up dinner from a place a few blocks away. He never came back. He was struck by a driver who ran a red light. Adama was the one who had to identify his body. She had stood in the morgue, unable to speak, her mouth open but no sound coming out. That was the moment that kept replaying, except she could never get to the end of it. Every time she tried to bring the memory into focus, she would push it away before it fully arrived, as if her mind slammed a door shut. She knew what had happened, but when her therapist asked her to describe it, she sat in silence, the words dissolving on her tongue. The memory did not feel like the past. It felt like it was happening right now, in the room, in her chest, and she would flinch as though the fluorescent lights of the lab were the harsh lights of the morgue.

In the months that followed, Adama began to live in a state of constant, low-grade alarm. She could not sleep. She would lie awake for hours, her mind circling the same question: why had she sent him out that night? She told herself that somebody else—a better sister, a more careful person—would have stopped it. She had come to believe that the event happened because of the sort of person she was: someone who did not protect the people she loved. The injustice of it burned in her. Nothing had been done. The driver had been charged, but the case had stalled, and the world kept moving as if Kofi had never existed. That was when she started picking fights. She would snap at a coworker for leaving a beaker unwashed. She would argue with her roommate about dishes until they both were shouting. She knew, even as she did it, that she was creating drama to distract herself from the weight she carried, but the weight was worse. The silence was worse.

At work, she began to notice small delays that had never bothered her before. When a sample result took an hour longer than expected, her heart would race and she would assume something catastrophic had happened—a spill, a contamination, a disaster. Her body reacted before her mind had time to catch up. She would find herself gripping the edge of her desk, breathing fast, before she even knew why. She stopped watching television or reading the news. Any story about a sudden death, any film with a character who lost someone, sent her into a spiral of intrusive images. She could not bear it. She avoided those programs the way she avoided the street where Kofi had died, taking a longer route home even though it added twenty minutes to her commute.

The consequences had accumulated quietly. Her relationships frayed. Her roommate asked to move out. Her supervisor noticed her irritability and recommended a leave of absence. What finally brought Adama to seek help was not the fights or the sleeplessness, but a moment in the lab when a colleague asked her a simple question about a data set and she could not find the words to answer. She stood there, mouth open, the same paralysis she had felt in the morgue, and she realized she was losing her ability to speak about anything at all. She was terrified that if she let herself remember fully, she would shatter. But she was also terrified of staying this way—of becoming someone who could not work, could not talk, could not stop blaming herself for the one thing she had never been able to control. She hoped, more than anything, that someone could help her find a way to tell the story without it destroying her.
